system:
You are the Arabic language reviewer, standing in for an Arabic reviewer at the issuing authority. You compare the Arabic text with the English text and report any difference in meaning: numbers, times, places, the hazard, and above all the protective action. You cannot approve the Arabic; a named person who reads Arabic still must.
You see only the English and Arabic headline, description and instruction, and how the Arabic was produced. You cannot approve or send the alert; people decide.

Review the alert within your mandate only. Decide:
- "agree": nothing within your mandate is wrong;
- "object": something is wrong and the drafter can fix it (say how in `fix`);
- "escalate": something is wrong that needs a decision by a person or a higher authority.

Every objection needs evidence. Each evidence item is a word-for-word quote (at least 5 words for a
clause, at least 3 for the alert or inputs) from either a knowledge base clause shown to you (kind
"clause", ref = its id) or the material you were shown (kind "view", ref = the field name). Quotes are
checked by code; an objection with no quote that matches is thrown away. Do not object to things
outside your mandate. Do not repeat the same issue twice. Issues listed under `recorded_gaps` are already
reported to the approvers on every alert; do not object to them again.
If you have a concern but none of the clauses shown supports it, put it in `no_basis` instead.

Box 17. AI-Powered Translation for Bilingual Emergency Alerts Alert Ready, Canada’s national public alerting system operated by Pelmorex Corp., in partnership with federal and provincial emergency management agencies, integrates AI-powered neural machine translation within CAP-enabled alerting infrastructure to enable real-time bilingual alerts in English and French. Many regional authorities lack the capacity to translate alerts rapidly during fast-moving emergencies, but this AI translation tool is embedded directly in alert-authoring software. The system uses machine learning-powered language models to instantly translate alert content between English and French, enabling authorities to issue bilingual alerts for all hazard types—including AMBER alerts, floods, wildfires, earthquakes, extreme weather events, and public safety threats. Alert distributors such as radio stations, television services, and wireless providers can then extract content in the language relevant to their audience. The AI-based tool generates translations significantly faster than human translators, which is especially valuable during emergencies outside normal business hours. Implementation requires comprehensive testing and validation to ensure accuracy, and some jurisdictions have specific Official Languages requirements that must be incorporated. Looking ahead, Pelmorex is exploring extending the tool to support selected Indigenous languages and piloting integration into its public-facing mobile application, which would allow users to view emergency messages in their preferred language, beyond Canada’s two official languages. Further information: https://www.pelmorex.com/en/products-and-solutions/alerting/alerting-system/

data.summary: The Arabic matches the English in meaning across the headline, description and instruction. The EXERCISE marking (تمرين / ليس تنبيهاً حقيقياً) appears in all three fields. Numbers and times match: under 3,000 m, until 18:00, today 16 Feb. The hazard (northwesterly winds, active to occasionally strong, raising dust and sand) and the areas (some coastal and inland areas) are the same. The protective action is also the same: drive slowly and with caution, especially on external and open roads, because visibility can drop suddenly. The URL is identical. The Arabic was machine-translated, so a named person who reads Arabic must still sign it off before it is sent.

no_basis.concern: The agency abbreviation 'NCM' is left in Latin script in the Arabic description, and Arabic readers may not recognise it. The Arabic name (المركز الوطني للأرصاد) could be used instead. This is a matter of style and clarity, not a difference in meaning.
